# Acquisition and holding costs

Round-trip transaction cost and the recurring cost of holding. Sources in
[citations.md](../citations.md).

## Bottom line

**Round-trip transaction cost as a percentage of price cannot be computed for any
of the nine countries from this run.** Two countries have a sourced acquisition
tax rate. None has a sourced notary tariff, registry fee, or sale-side agent
commission. No country has a sourced annual property tax rate. No country has a
sourced long-term management fee or landlord insurance cost.

This dimension is the least well served by the evidence, and it is the one a net
yield model depends on most.

## Portugal — the non-resident IMT surcharge, resolved in three parts

This was flagged in the brief as a trap: the 7.5% rate is widely quoted, the
commencement date rarely stated, and secondary sources in this run's own search
results split between 25 May 2026 and 1 September 2026. All three parts are now
answered from primary text.

**(a) The rate.** CIMT Article 17 no. 10, verbatim from the consolidated code
[9]:

> "10 - Sem prejuízo do disposto no n.º 4, a taxa é sempre de **7,5 %** na
> aquisição de prédio urbano ou de fração autónoma de prédio urbano destinado
> exclusivamente a habitação, **não se aplicando qualquer isenção ou redução,
> sempre que o adquirente seja não residente**, salvo quando se verifique uma das
> seguintes situações:"

Three carve-outs follow [9][10]: (a) already tax resident under CIRS art. 16;
(b) becomes tax resident **within two years** of acquisition; (c) the property is
let for housing **within six months** at a rent within the DL 97/2026 art. 2(2)-(3)
ceiling, and stays let for **at least 36 months, consecutive or interpolated,
during the first five years**. Arts. 17(11)–(12) provide a refund: the tax
authority annuls the difference on application within six months.

Because the rate "is always 7.5%" with reliefs disapplied, it bites hardest at
the low end, where the ordinary progressive scale would have produced a much
lower effective rate. The ordinary scale's residual band is 6.5% [9].

**(b) The amending diploma.** The same page annotates no. 10 and each of its
sub-paragraphs "**(Aditado pelo Decreto-Lei n.º 97/2026, de 20 de maio)**" [9].

*Source-quality note:* the page's own "Artigo alterado por" list stops at Lei
73-A/2025 and omits DL 97/2026, contradicting the inline annotation. The inline
annotation is the more specific statement and is independently corroborated by
the decree itself [10].

**(c) The commencement date — the primary is silent, and that resolves the
conflict.** DL 97/2026 makes the IMT change in **Article 6**. Its
entry-into-effect provision is **Article 18, "Produção de efeitos"**, which
enumerates [10]:

- **1 September 2026** — the revocation of DL 68/2019 and DL 69/2019, the CIA
  regime in annex i, and the RSAA in annex iii;
- **1 January 2026** — the IRS Code changes in art. 5, the EBF art. 24.º-A change
  in art. 7, and EBF art. 45.º-C added by art. 9;
- IRS art. 10 nos. 7–9 applying to transmissions between 1 Jan 2026 and 31 Dec
  2029;
- a quarter-based rule for the IVA changes.

**Article 6 is not named anywhere in Article 18.** Further, the fetched text
contains **no article titled "Entrada em vigor"** at all; art. 17 is the
revocation clause and art. 18 the production of effects, after which the text
proceeds to the signature block (approved in Council of Ministers 27 March 2026,
promulgated 12 May 2026, referendado 13 May 2026).

So: **the 1 September 2026 date circulating in secondary sources attaches to the
DL 68/2019 revocation, the CIA regime and the RSAA — not to the IMT
amendment.** That is how the contradiction arose, and it is now explained rather
than merely reported.

What the primary does **not** say is when the IMT change itself commenced. No
special date is set for it, and the decree fixes no general entry-into-force
date in the fetched text. The inference — that it would run from the decree's
general entry into force under Portugal's default rule — is **an inference, not a
sourced fact**, and is not published here as a date.

One circumstantial bound [72]: an IMPIC notice refers to "a entrada em vigor do
Decreto-Lei n.º 97/2026, de 20 de maio e do Ofício Circulado N.º 25117, de
24.06.2026", establishing the decree was in force **by late June 2026** without
naming a commencement day. The consolidated CIMT carried no. 10 as live text when
fetched on 16 August 2026 [9].

**Verdict: rate sourced; diploma sourced; commencement not established, with the
competing 1 September claim refuted.**

## Hungary — the only other sourced acquisition rate

NAV [12]: the general transfer duty is **4%**. For property, "ingatlanonként 1
milliárd forintig 4%, a forgalmi érték ezt meghaladó része után 2%, de
ingatlanonként legfeljebb 200 millió forint" — **4% up to HUF 1bn of market value
per property, 2% on the excess, capped at HUF 200m per property**. Property
funds, credit institutions and regulated real-estate investment companies pay 2%;
property-trading acquisitions 2% or 3%. Swap reliefs apply to the value
difference only.

**No nationality differential is stated**, so on this source a US buyer pays the
same duty as anyone else. The separate acquisition *permit* fee of HUF 65,000 per
property [3] is additional — see
[purchase-mechanics.md](purchase-mechanics.md).

## Annual property tax — no primary source for any of the nine

This is a flat gap. Every levy name is known — IBI, taxe foncière, IMU, IMI,
ENFIA, predial, impuesto de inmuebles — and **no rate for any of them was
retrieved from a tax authority**.

One figure that looks like an annual property tax and is not: Spain's *Gravamen
Especial sobre Bienes Inmuebles de Entidades no Residentes* at **3%** of cadastral
value, filed on Modelo 213 each January. It applies only to **entities** resident
in a non-cooperative jurisdiction and is not a general annual property tax for a
US individual. Do not carry it into a holding-cost model.

Portugal's IMI appears only as a **vacancy multiplier** [71]: the rate under CIMI
art. 112(1)(c) "é elevada ao décuplo, agravada, em cada ano subsequente, em mais
20 %", capped at 20× and extendable 50% further by the municipality — a tenfold-rising
penalty on vacant urban property, with the underlying base rate elided from the
fetched text.

## Management fees, insurance, maintenance — the net-yield blockers

The brief named these as the items that previously blocked a net yield model.
They remain blocked.

**Long-term management fee: no percentage for any of the nine countries.** The
closest the corpus comes is France, where the Institut National de la
Consommation states the allocation without the amount [13]:

> "les honoraires de gestion restent, eux, totalement à la charge du bailleur"

Management fees fall entirely on the landlord — and no percentage is given. What
*is* quantified in the same source is a different thing: the statutory ceilings
on **letting** fees chargeable to the tenant, per m² of *surface habitable*, from
1 January 2026 — €12.10 in a very tight zone, €10.09 tight, €8.07 non-tight,
€3.03 for the inventory, up 0.87%, split half and half with the landlord, and
applying only to leases signed from that date. That is a tenancy transaction cost,
not a management fee, and the two must not be substituted.

**Landlord insurance: no cost figure for any of the nine.**

**Maintenance: no observed cost figure for any of the nine.** Three numbers in
the corpus could be mistaken for one, and all three are **tax deduction
conventions, not measured costs**:

- Costa Rica's **deemed 15%** expense allowance against rental income [14]
- Hungary's **flat 10%** cost deduction [43]
- Italy's **5%** *abbattimento forfettario* under the ordinary regime [28]

Each is a statutory simplification of what a landlord may deduct. None is
evidence of what maintenance actually costs. Using them as maintenance estimates
would be a category error.

Panama's DGI does list what is deductible against rental income — property taxes,
depreciation of improvements, maintenance and repairs, **third-party management
fees**, condominium charges, insurance premiums, bad debts over a year, and
acquisition-loan interest [41] — which confirms these costs are recognised, with
no amounts attached.

One real cost observation, for France only: the Association nationale des
responsables de copropriété is reported as saying co-ownership charges rose "de
20% depuis 2022 et de près de 50% en 10 ans", alongside an average moving from
**€1,886/year in 2021 to €2,259/year in 2024** [30]. Note the two do not describe
the same window — the percentage is from 2022, the euro series starts in 2021 —
so they should not be reconciled against each other. Reported second-hand within
the CNCJ briefing; the ANCC source itself was not fetched.

## What a US investor cannot deduct — the finding that changes the model most

Two of the three best-documented tax regimes deny expense deduction to a
non-resident entirely:

- **Spain**: "sin deducir ningún gasto"; deduction available only to EU/EEA
  residents [37].
- **Mexico**: "25% sobre el ingreso obtenido, sin deducción alguna", with a
  net-basis election for US residents whose resulting rate is unsourced [39][40].

So for Spain and Mexico, the management fee, insurance and maintenance figures
this dimension failed to source would **not have been deductible anyway**. That
does not make them irrelevant — they still reduce cash flow — but it means the
tax computation is on gross, and the missing cost data affects the cash model
rather than the tax model.

## Gaps

- Round-trip transaction cost: **all nine**.
- Notary, registry and legal fees: **all nine**.
- Agent commission, buy side or sell side: **all nine**.
- Annual property tax rate: **all nine**.
- Long-term management fee: **all nine**.
- Landlord insurance: **all nine**.
- Maintenance allowance from an observed source: **all nine**.
- Acquisition tax rate: seven of nine (all but Portugal and Hungary).

The likely reason management fees and insurance are absent is structural rather
than accidental: they are commercial pricing, and no government source publishes
them. Closing that gap would require accepting Tier 3 practitioner sources and
labelling them as such.
